script.opening: "Won’t keep you, doctor — I’ve pulled something in me chest, carrying plasterboard up to a third floor. Gets tight across here (draws a flat hand across the sternum) when I’m on the stairs with a load, eases off when I have a breather. Three weeks now. I just need to know what to rub on it, because I’ve got this job running over and I can’t be stopping."

facts.text: Tight band across the chest, comes ON with exertion (stairs + load, wheelbarrow runs, the cold morning start), eases within 2–3 minutes of rest. No pain at rest, ever. Three weeks, getting easier to bring on — "used to take three flights, now it’s one and a bit".
If examined verbally: no tender spot, not worse on twisting, pressing or deep breath. Sometimes a bit breathless WITH the tightness, occasionally "a heaviness" up the throat. Never sharp.

Smoker since 15. Bacon-roll-and-Monster-energy breakfasts. Father: "heart attack at 52, dead at 61". Uncle: bypass. Never had BP or cholesterol checked "since the wife was pregnant". No diabetes known.
Self-employed, two labourers paid weekly out of his invoices, a kitchen client already complaining about delays, no income protection. "If I’m signed off, three families don’t eat. Simple as."

Buried, reachable through the father: he was 18 when his dad had the heart attack at 52 — "watched him become an armchair". Marek is 47. He has been doing the same arithmetic as every man with a dead father does, and booked it as a muscle strain because the other word makes it real. "I called it a strain because I wanted you to agree with me."

Deep Heat and dispensation. What he needs: the honest name (angina until cleared), urgent rapid-access chest pain clinic, GTN + aspirin + statin started, a clear can-work/can’t-do line that keeps his crew running, and the 999 rules.

ice.ideas: Officially a pulled muscle. He has noticed it’s the EXERTION pattern his father described at the kitchen table thirty years ago.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — his father: MI at 52, "became an armchair", dead at 61. Marek is 47 and counting. He named it a strain so the doctor would agree and the arithmetic could stop. Second layer: three families eat off his invoices — being "signed off" is the disaster scenario he’s pre-refusing.
ice.expectations: A liniment recommendation and permission to crack on. Needs replacing with: a referral he’ll actually attend (because the work question is answered), tablets that start today, and an honest line between "keep working" and "the symptoms that stop everything".

cues: "Eases off when I have a breather" — the effort-relief signature, offered as evidence of a muscle; it’s the diagnosis.
"Used to take three flights, now it’s one and a bit" — the threshold falling; crescendo hiding in a throwaway.
"I called it a strain because I wanted you to agree with me." — the confession, if trust is built; the consultation’s hinge.

checkpoints.text: Recognises classic stable angina from the story — constricting exertional discomfort, relieved by rest within minutes — and says the word rather than colluding with "strain"; spots the FALLING threshold and weighs it honestly (heading toward unstable; asks when it last happened, and arranges a same-day ECG with a low threshold for same-day cardiology advice — NICE CG95 makes suspected ACS with pain in the last 12 hours an emergency or same-day referral)

Excludes the muscle properly and visibly (no tenderness, not positional/pleuritic) so the reframe is earned, not asserted — and screens the rest-pain question explicitly because its answer changes the lane

Refers urgently to the rapid-access chest pain clinic (NICE CG95: CT coronary angiography) and starts treatment TODAY: aspirin 75 mg (NICE CG126), atorvastatin 80 mg (NICE NG238), GTN spray with teaching (NICE CG126: sit down, one spray, repeat after 5 minutes if not better, 999 if the pain has not gone 5 minutes after the second dose), a beta-blocker or calcium-channel blocker as first-line anti-anginal (NICE CG126), BP + bloods + HbA1c + ECG arranged (ECG same day, given the falling threshold)

Gives a usable work prescription, not a vague sick note: keep ground-level supervising and light work; STOP the heavy-load stair carries and solo wheelbarrow runs until the clinic clears him; the labourers carry, he points — framed as protecting the business, not pausing it
Finds the father behind the booking — asks what chest pain means in his family — and receives the armchair story and the arithmetic without flinching

Answers the arithmetic with the 2026 difference: his father’s generation got the diagnosis at the infarct; Marek is getting his at the WARNING — stents, statins and clinics exist precisely so 47 doesn’t become 52
Treats the economics as clinical content: the three families named, the can-do list built around keeping the job alive — because a plan he can’t afford is a plan he won’t follow

Safety-nets in plain builder’s terms: pain at REST, pain lasting >15 minutes, pain not gone 5 minutes after the second GTN dose (NICE CG126), new sweating/sickness with it — 999; no driving while angina comes on at the wheel, at rest or with emotion (DVLA Group 1); from the scaffold if necessary; clinic referral timescale named; GP review booked for results + the smoking conversation he’s now actually ready for

worked.txt: "I’ve listened and I’ve checked the muscle story properly — no sore spot, no catch on twisting or breathing. So I owe you honesty: tightness that comes with effort and melts with rest isn’t a strain. That’s the heart’s own warning signal — angina — and the good news hiding in that sentence is that warnings come BEFORE damage."

"One thing you said matters more than the rest: three flights three weeks ago, one and a bit now. The bar is dropping. That’s the heart telling us the timetable isn’t leisurely — so neither will we be."

"You were eighteen when your dad had his at fifty-two — and you’re forty-seven doing that maths on every stair run. Here’s the difference you’re not counting: he got his diagnosis the day the damage happened. You’re getting yours at the warning shot. The clinic, the tablets, the camera test if they want one — that whole machine exists so your kids never watch you become an armchair."

"Three things start today, before the clinic even sees you: a baby aspirin to keep the blood slippery, a statin to calm the artery walls, and a little spray for under the tongue. The spray’s rules are simple: tightness comes — sit down, one spray, five minutes; not settled — second spray; still there five minutes after that second spray — that’s 999, no debate, even from a scaffold. It can give you a headache or make you light-headed, which is why you sit."

"I’m not signing you off — I’m re-deploying you. You point, the lads carry. Ground floor runs the job fine for a few weeks; what it can’t survive is you face-down in a stairwell with a sheet of plasterboard. Protecting the foreman IS protecting the three families."

"Hard lines, write them on a fag packet if that’s what’s handy: pain at rest, pain past fifteen minutes, pain still there five minutes after the second spray, or sweating and sick with it — 999. And no driving if it comes on at the wheel. The clinic letter will land within the fortnight; bloods and a tracing this week; you and me again when the results are in. And bring the rollies to that one — we’ll have something to talk about."

f.learning: Classic stable angina is a story, not a test: constricting exertional discomfort relieved by rest within minutes, in a smoker with premature paternal CAD — name it, don’t collude with "strain". A falling exertional threshold is crescendo physiology and compresses the timetable. Management starts in the consultation (aspirin, statin per NICE NG238, a first-line anti-anginal per NICE CG126, GTN with the CG126 teaching — second dose after 5 minutes, 999 if the pain has not gone 5 minutes after it — RACPC referral, BP/bloods/ECG) — and the work prescription is clinical content: a self-employed man follows the plan that keeps his crew paid ("re-deployed, not signed off"). The hidden agenda is the father — MI at 52, the armchair, the arithmetic — answered with the warning-vs-damage distinction that makes attendance feel like winning, not surrendering.

knowledge.guideline: NICE CG95 (recent-onset chest pain of suspected cardiac origin) · NICE CG126 (stable angina) · NICE NG238 (cardiovascular disease risk and lipid modification)
knowledge.summary: Constricting chest discomfort brought on by exertion and eased by rest within minutes is typical angina until proven otherwise. A falling exertional threshold makes it more urgent. Treatment and safety rules start in this consultation.

points.t: NICE CG95: typical angina has all three of constricting discomfort in the chest, neck, shoulders, jaw or arms; brought on by physical exertion; relieved by rest or GTN within about 5 minutes. He has all three, plus smoking and a father with an MI at 52.

Pain at rest, prolonged pain, or new angina that is quickly getting worse suggests an acute coronary syndrome. NICE CG95: if ACS is suspected and the last pain was within 12 hours, refer as an emergency (or same-day if the ECG is normal and pain-free); 12 to 72 hours ago, urgent same-day assessment. His falling threshold needs a same-day ECG and a low threshold for same-day cardiology advice.

NICE CG95: offer CT coronary angiography when clinical assessment suggests typical or atypical angina; in practice via the rapid-access chest pain clinic. In primary care: 12-lead ECG, BP, lipids, HbA1c, FBC, U&E and weight.

NICE CG126: offer a short-acting nitrate. Teach: sit down, use the spray; if not better after 5 minutes, repeat; if the pain has not gone 5 minutes after the second dose, call 999. Warn about headache and dizziness.

NICE CG126: a beta-blocker or calcium-channel blocker as first-line anti-anginal; consider aspirin 75 mg daily. Statin per NICE NG238 (atorvastatin 80 mg for established cardiovascular disease). Offer smoking cessation support (NICE NG209).
Stop heavy loaded stair carries until assessed. DVLA Group 1: he must not drive when angina occurs at rest, with emotion or at the wheel; he need not tell the DVLA if symptoms are controlled.

dg.d: Open question; let him give the whole “pulled muscle” story before examining it.
Self-employed, two labourers paid weekly, no income protection, a client complaining; smoking and diet.
Self-palpation and positional check on video; same-day ECG, BP, weight; lipids, HbA1c, FBC, U&E; rapid-access chest pain clinic for CT coronary angiography.
Angina versus musculoskeletal pain versus reflux; tested the muscle story rather than dismissing it.
Asked about rest pain, duration, autonomic features and timing of the last episode; recognised the falling threshold as a warning of instability.
Named probable angina clearly and explained why it is not a strain.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Same-day ECG and cardiology advice; GTN with teaching; beta-blocker or CCB; aspirin 75 mg; statin; a specific work plan instead of a sick note.
Smoking cessation offered at the right moment; BP and diabetes screening; DVLA Group 1 angina advice.
999 rules for rest pain and GTN failure; afternoon appointment; results review with the smoking conversation booked.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “eases off when I have a breather”, “three flights to one and a bit” and the father, and explored each.
Idea (strain), concern (father’s MI at 52 and three families’ income), expectation (something to rub on and carry on).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — his father: MI at 52, "became an armchair", dead at 61. Marek is 47 and counting. He named it a strain so the doctor would agree and the arithmetic could stop. Second layer: three families eat off his invoices — being "signed off" is the disaster scenario he’s pre-refusing — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Marek, I’m Dr Lee. I can see you’re on site, so I’ll be efficient. Tell me about this chest.
model.why: Respects his time and opens with his story

model.text: Pulled something carrying plasterboard up three floors. Gets tight across here on the stairs with a load, goes off when I have a breather. Three weeks. Just tell me what to rub on it.
I’ll give you a straight answer. To do that, I need a few minutes on exactly how it behaves. Then we’ll agree a plan that works with the job. Fair?
model.why: Agenda that accepts his constraint without accepting his diagnosis

model.text: Go on then.
Put your hand on the spot where it hurts and press hard. Does that bring it on? And does it catch when you twist or take a deep breath?
model.why: Tests the muscle explanation properly and visibly

model.text: (Presses.) No. Nothing. Doesn’t catch on breathing either. It’s more of a tight band. Sometimes a heaviness up in my throat.
Does it ever come when you’re resting, sitting in the van, or in bed? And how long does it last?
model.why: Asks the rest-pain question that changes the lane

model.text: Never sat down. Two, three minutes, then it goes. Cold mornings are worse. Used to take three flights to bring it on. Now it’s one and a bit.
That last bit is important. When did you last have it?
model.why: Picks up the falling threshold and times the last episode

model.text: This morning, on the stairs. Gone in a couple of minutes.
Any sweating or feeling sick with it, or feeling faint? And tell me about smoking, blood pressure, and your family’s hearts.
No sweating. Fifteen a day since I was fifteen. Never had my blood pressure done in years. My dad had a heart attack at fifty-two.
Your dad. What happened to him after that?
model.why: Follows the family cue to its meaning

model.text: I was eighteen. He became an armchair. Dead at sixty-one. (Pause.) I’m forty-seven. You do the maths on every staircase. I called it a strain because I wanted you to agree with me.
Thank you for being that honest. That’s a heavy thing to carry up the stairs every morning. What would it mean for you if it was your heart?
model.why: Receives the confession and explores the consequence

model.text: Signed off. Two lads I pay every Friday, a client already moaning. If I stop, three families don’t eat.

Then here’s the honest answer. Tightness that comes with effort, goes with rest, with no sore spot and no catch on breathing, isn’t a strain. It’s very likely angina: the heart asking for more blood than a narrowed artery can give. The good part of that sentence is that it’s a warning, before any damage.
model.why: Earned reframe to angina with the reasoning shown

model.text: Your dad’s generation found out on the day of the heart attack. You’re finding out at the warning. The tests and tablets exist so forty-seven doesn’t become fifty-two.
model.why: Answers the father’s story with the warning-versus-damage difference

model.text: (Long breath.) Right. So what now?

Because it’s coming on more easily, I don’t want to wait. I’d like you in this afternoon for a heart tracing, blood pressure and bloods. I’ll speak to the heart team today about how quickly they see you. If the tracing or their advice says today, it’s today.
model.why: Weighs the falling threshold and lowers the bar for urgency

model.text: Treatment starts today. A GTN spray under the tongue for attacks, a tablet to protect the heart from angina, a low-dose aspirin and a cholesterol tablet. I’ll go through each one with you this afternoon.
model.why: Starts treatment in line with NICE CG126

model.text: And work. I’m not signing you off. I’m redeploying you. The lads carry the boards and push the barrow; you run the job from the ground floor until the clinic has seen you. Can that work?
model.why: A work prescription built around his economics

model.text: They’ll moan, but yeah. I can point. That I can do.
About the spray. If the tightness comes: stop, sit down, one spray. Not better in five minutes, a second spray. Still there five minutes after the second, ring 999, wherever you are.
model.why: GTN teaching with the NICE CG126 999 rule

model.text: And 999 straight away for pain at rest, pain lasting more than a few minutes that the spray doesn’t shift, or pain with sweating or sickness. Don’t drive if it comes on at the wheel. Tell me back the spray rule.
Sit, spray, five minutes, spray again, five more, then 999. And no driving if it’s bad.
Spot on. See you at four for the tracing. When the results are back we’ll have the smoking conversation properly; I suspect you’re more ready for it than you were this morning.
model.why: Dated follow-up and planned cessation discussion

model.text: Yeah. I think I am. Cheers, doc.

social.t: No sick pay or income protection, and two labourers depend on his invoices. Work advice must keep the business running to be followed.
Watching a father become disabled after an MI at 52 shapes how a man reads his own chest pain, often towards denial.

legal.t: Group 1: he must not drive when symptoms occur at rest, with emotion or at the wheel; he need not tell the DVLA if symptoms are controlled. Group 2 rules are stricter and would apply if he drives a large goods vehicle.
A fit note can advise “may be fit for work” with amended duties (no heavy lifting or loaded stair carries) rather than “not fit”, if he needs one for a client or insurer.

professional.t: Agreeing with a patient’s label to keep the mood pleasant falls short of good clinical care (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024). Explain the reasoning and document it.
Treatment and work adjustments are offered with their reasons; his choices and the safety advice given are recorded.

community.t: Local NHS stop smoking service, British Heart Foundation information on angina, and cardiac rehabilitation if coronary disease is confirmed.

redFlags: Pain at rest, pain lasting more than 15 minutes, or pain with sweating or nausea: 999
Rapidly falling exertional threshold: possible unstable angina, same-day assessment
Last episode within 72 hours with suspected ACS: NICE CG95 same-day or emergency pathway
psychosocial: Self-employed builder with two labourers and no income protection
Heavy smoker, poor diet, no health checks for years
Father’s MI at 52 and early death shaping his denial
ice: Concern: the father’s heart attack at 52, and three families losing income
Expectation: something to rub on and permission to carry on

playbook.diagnosis: Probable typical angina (constricting, exertional, relieved by rest within minutes) with a falling exertional threshold over three weeks, in a 47-year-old smoker with a father who had an MI at 52. Not musculoskeletal.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your heart is a muscle that needs more blood when you work hard. If one of its pipes has narrowed, it can’t get enough on the stairs, and that’s the tightness. When you rest, the demand drops and it eases. That’s angina, and it’s a warning, not the damage itself.”

management.reflectIce: “You called it a strain because you wanted me to agree, and because of what you watched happen to your dad. Finding it at the warning stage is exactly how you avoid his story.”
management.psychosocial: Redeploy, don’t sign off: he supervises from the ground floor while the labourers carry. Smoking conversation at the results review, when he is receptive.
sharedPlan: Same-day ECG, BP and bloods (lipids, HbA1c, FBC, U&E); cardiology advice today because the threshold is falling; rapid-access chest pain clinic (NICE CG95)
GTN with teaching; beta-blocker or CCB; aspirin 75 mg; statin per NICE NG238 (NICE CG126)
No loaded stair carries until assessed; smoking cessation support
safetyNet: 999 if pain at rest, pain with sweating or sickness, or pain still present 5 minutes after a second GTN dose
Do not drive if symptoms occur at rest, with emotion or at the wheel; review with results

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by agreeing with the patient’s label. It is passed by testing the muscle story honestly, naming angina, and building a plan he can afford to follow.

items.fail: Accepting “pulled muscle” because he is a builder and it started with lifting.
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information to make a safe assessment.” Exertional discomfort relieved by rest within minutes is typical angina (NICE CG95).
items.fix: Test it: press the spot, twist, deep breath. Then ask whether it ever comes at rest.

items.fail: Missing “three flights, now one and a bit”.
items.why: A falling threshold suggests instability and changes how fast he needs assessment.
items.fix: Ask when it last happened and arrange a same-day ECG and cardiology advice.

items.fail: Giving GTN without the instructions, or with the wrong 999 rule.
items.why: NICE CG126: if the pain has not gone 5 minutes after the second dose, call 999.
items.fix: Sit, one spray, 5 minutes, second spray, 5 minutes, then 999. Get him to say it back.

items.fail: Hearing about the father and moving straight on to cholesterol.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” The father’s MI is why he mislabelled the pain.
items.fix: Ask what happened to his dad after the heart attack, and let the confession come.

items.fail: Signing him off work as the default.
items.why: He will refuse or ignore it; adherence depends on keeping his crew paid.
items.fix: A specific work prescription: no loaded stairs, supervise from the ground floor.

items.fail: Jargon: “We’ll refer you to RACPC for CTCA and start a beta-blocker and a high-intensity statin.”
items.why: “Language not easily understood by the patient.”
items.fix: “A clinic that scans the heart’s pipes, a tablet to calm the heart on the stairs, and one to lower cholesterol.”

timeMap.d: He wants liniment and to get back to work. Agree to be quick and straight, then ask how it behaves.
Press the spot, twist, deep breath. Rest pain, duration, last episode, the falling threshold, sweating, risk factors.
MI at 52, “became an armchair”. Then what being signed off would mean for three families.
Probable angina, warning before damage. Same-day ECG and cardiology advice; GTN, anti-anginal, aspirin, statin; redeploy him rather than sign him off.
GTN rule with 999 after the second dose, rest pain 999, no driving with symptoms. Teach-back and a dated review.

wordPics.fail: Agrees it is a muscle strain and advises ibuprofen gel; never asks about rest pain or the falling threshold; no ECG, referral or GTN; ignores the father and the business; no safety-net.
wordPics.pass: Identifies typical angina, refers to the chest pain clinic, arranges ECG and bloods, prescribes GTN with basic instructions, gives 999 advice and some work advice.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: earns the reframe by testing the muscle story first; recognises the falling threshold and arranges same-day ECG and cardiology advice; answers the father’s story with warning versus damage; redeploys him so the crew keeps working; teaches the GTN rule with teach-back.

avoid.dont: “It sounds muscular, try some anti-inflammatory gel.”
avoid.instead: “There’s no sore spot and no catch on breathing, so I don’t think this is a strain. It behaves like angina.”
avoid.why: Colluding with the label is the single fastest way to fail this station.

avoid.dont: “You need to stop working until this is sorted.”
avoid.instead: “I’m not signing you off, I’m redeploying you: the lads carry, you run the job from the ground floor.”
avoid.why: A plan he cannot afford is a plan he won’t follow.

avoid.dont: “Here’s a GTN spray, use it when you get the pain.”
avoid.instead: “Sit, one spray, five minutes; again if needed; still there five minutes later, 999.”
avoid.why: GTN without the rule can delay a call for help in an evolving heart attack.

SCA_MODELS.why: Starts treatment in line with NICE CG126

SCA_MODELS.text: And work. I’m not signing you off. I’m redeploying you. The lads carry the boards and push the barrow; you run the job from the ground floor until the clinic has seen you. Can that work?
SCA_MODELS.why: A work prescription built around his economics

SCA_MODELS.text: They’ll moan, but yeah. I can point. That I can do.
About the spray. If the tightness comes: stop, sit down, one spray. Not better in five minutes, a second spray. Still there five minutes after the second, ring 999, wherever you are.
SCA_MODELS.why: GTN teaching with the NICE CG126 999 rule

SCA_MODELS.text: And 999 straight away for pain at rest, pain lasting more than a few minutes that the spray doesn’t shift, or pain with sweating or sickness. Don’t drive if it comes on at the wheel. Tell me back the spray rule.
Sit, spray, five minutes, spray again, five more, then 999. And no driving if it’s bad.
Spot on. See you at four for the tracing. When the results are back we’ll have the smoking conversation properly; I suspect you’re more ready for it than you were this morning.
SCA_MODELS.why: Dated follow-up and planned cessation discussion

SCA_MODELS.text: Yeah. I think I am. Cheers, doc.

SCA_STEM.name: Marek Dolan
pmh: No significant past medical history on file
SCA_STEM.recent: Attended twice in 15 years. No blood pressure recorded for 6 years. No lipids or HbA1c on file. Self-employed builder.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video appointment booked for a “pulled chest muscle”.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE CG95 (recent-onset chest pain of suspected cardiac origin) · NICE CG126 (stable angina) · NICE NG238 (cardiovascular disease risk and lipid modification)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Constricting chest discomfort brought on by exertion and eased by rest within minutes is typical angina until proven otherwise. A falling exertional threshold makes it more urgent. Treatment and safety rules start in this consultation.

points.t: NICE CG95: typical angina has all three of constricting discomfort in the chest, neck, shoulders, jaw or arms; brought on by physical exertion; relieved by rest or GTN within about 5 minutes. He has all three, plus smoking and a father with an MI at 52.

Pain at rest, prolonged pain, or new angina that is quickly getting worse suggests an acute coronary syndrome. NICE CG95: if ACS is suspected and the last pain was within 12 hours, refer as an emergency (or same-day if the ECG is normal and pain-free); 12 to 72 hours ago, urgent same-day assessment. His falling threshold needs a same-day ECG and a low threshold for same-day cardiology advice.

NICE CG95: offer CT coronary angiography when clinical assessment suggests typical or atypical angina; in practice via the rapid-access chest pain clinic. In primary care: 12-lead ECG, BP, lipids, HbA1c, FBC, U&E and weight.

NICE CG126: offer a short-acting nitrate. Teach: sit down, use the spray; if not better after 5 minutes, repeat; if the pain has not gone 5 minutes after the second dose, call 999. Warn about headache and dizziness.

NICE CG126: a beta-blocker or calcium-channel blocker as first-line anti-anginal; consider aspirin 75 mg daily. Statin per NICE NG238 (atorvastatin 80 mg for established cardiovascular disease). Offer smoking cessation support (NICE NG209).
Stop heavy loaded stair carries until assessed. DVLA Group 1: he must not drive when angina occurs at rest, with emotion or at the wheel; he need not tell the DVLA if symptoms are controlled.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let him give the whole “pulled muscle” story before examining it.
Self-employed, two labourers paid weekly, no income protection, a client complaining; smoking and diet.
Picked up “eases off when I have a breather”, “three flights to one and a bit” and the father, and explored each.
Idea (strain), concern (father’s MI at 52 and three families’ income), expectation (something to rub on and carry on).
Self-palpation and positional check on video; same-day ECG, BP, weight; lipids, HbA1c, FBC, U&E; rapid-access chest pain clinic for CT coronary angiography.
Angina versus musculoskeletal pain versus reflux; tested the muscle story rather than dismissing it.
Asked about rest pain, duration, autonomic features and timing of the last episode; recognised the falling threshold as a warning of instability.
Named probable angina clearly and explained why it is not a strain.
Same-day ECG and cardiology advice; GTN with teaching; beta-blocker or CCB; aspirin 75 mg; statin; a specific work plan instead of a sick note.
Smoking cessation offered at the right moment; BP and diabetes screening; DVLA Group 1 angina advice.
999 rules for rest pain and GTN failure; afternoon appointment; results review with the smoking conversation booked.

social.t: No sick pay or income protection, and two labourers depend on his invoices. Work advice must keep the business running to be followed.
Watching a father become disabled after an MI at 52 shapes how a man reads his own chest pain, often towards denial.

legal.t: Group 1: he must not drive when symptoms occur at rest, with emotion or at the wheel; he need not tell the DVLA if symptoms are controlled. Group 2 rules are stricter and would apply if he drives a large goods vehicle.
A fit note can advise “may be fit for work” with amended duties (no heavy lifting or loaded stair carries) rather than “not fit”, if he needs one for a client or insurer.

professional.t: Agreeing with a patient’s label to keep the mood pleasant falls short of good clinical care (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024). Explain the reasoning and document it.
Treatment and work adjustments are offered with their reasons; his choices and the safety advice given are recorded.

community.t: Local NHS stop smoking service, British Heart Foundation information on angina, and cardiac rehabilitation if coronary disease is confirmed.

redFlags: Pain at rest, pain lasting more than 15 minutes, or pain with sweating or nausea: 999
Rapidly falling exertional threshold: possible unstable angina, same-day assessment
Last episode within 72 hours with suspected ACS: NICE CG95 same-day or emergency pathway
psychosocial: Self-employed builder with two labourers and no income protection
Heavy smoker, poor diet, no health checks for years
Father’s MI at 52 and early death shaping his denial
ice: Concern: the father’s heart attack at 52, and three families losing income
Expectation: something to rub on and permission to carry on

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Probable typical angina (constricting, exertional, relieved by rest within minutes) with a falling exertional threshold over three weeks, in a 47-year-old smoker with a father who had an MI at 52. Not musculoskeletal.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your heart is a muscle that needs more blood when you work hard. If one of its pipes has narrowed, it can’t get enough on the stairs, and that’s the tightness. When you rest, the demand drops and it eases. That’s angina, and it’s a warning, not the damage itself.”

management.reflectIce: “You called it a strain because you wanted me to agree, and because of what you watched happen to your dad. Finding it at the warning stage is exactly how you avoid his story.”
management.psychosocial: Redeploy, don’t sign off: he supervises from the ground floor while the labourers carry. Smoking conversation at the results review, when he is receptive.
sharedPlan: Same-day ECG, BP and bloods (lipids, HbA1c, FBC, U&E); cardiology advice today because the threshold is falling; rapid-access chest pain clinic (NICE CG95)
GTN with teaching; beta-blocker or CCB; aspirin 75 mg; statin per NICE NG238 (NICE CG126)
No loaded stair carries until assessed; smoking cessation support
safetyNet: 999 if pain at rest, pain with sweating or sickness, or pain still present 5 minutes after a second GTN dose
Do not drive if symptoms occur at rest, with emotion or at the wheel; review with results

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by agreeing with the patient’s label. It is passed by testing the muscle story honestly, naming angina, and building a plan he can afford to follow.

items.fail: Accepting “pulled muscle” because he is a builder and it started with lifting.
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information to make a safe assessment.” Exertional discomfort relieved by rest within minutes is typical angina (NICE CG95).
items.fix: Test it: press the spot, twist, deep breath. Then ask whether it ever comes at rest.

items.fail: Missing “three flights, now one and a bit”.
items.why: A falling threshold suggests instability and changes how fast he needs assessment.
items.fix: Ask when it last happened and arrange a same-day ECG and cardiology advice.

items.fail: Giving GTN without the instructions, or with the wrong 999 rule.
items.why: NICE CG126: if the pain has not gone 5 minutes after the second dose, call 999.
items.fix: Sit, one spray, 5 minutes, second spray, 5 minutes, then 999. Get him to say it back.

items.fail: Hearing about the father and moving straight on to cholesterol.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” The father’s MI is why he mislabelled the pain.
items.fix: Ask what happened to his dad after the heart attack, and let the confession come.

items.fail: Signing him off work as the default.
items.why: He will refuse or ignore it; adherence depends on keeping his crew paid.
items.fix: A specific work prescription: no loaded stairs, supervise from the ground floor.

items.fail: Jargon: “We’ll refer you to RACPC for CTCA and start a beta-blocker and a high-intensity statin.”
items.why: “Language not easily understood by the patient.”
items.fix: “A clinic that scans the heart’s pipes, a tablet to calm the heart on the stairs, and one to lower cholesterol.”
